title: No Model Required: Text Entropy Rate Filtering Prevents Iterative Fine-Tuning Collapse
claim: Filtering training data on a model-free text statistic preserves diversity across iterative generations, while model-probability-based filtering gives no significant benefit.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right: line trend over generations, then grouped bars with significance stars
description: Two side-by-side plots share one color code: orange for unfiltered, blue for the logprob-based filter (H_L), and green for the entropy-rate filter (Ĥ_K). Panel (a) is a line chart of entropy rate in bits per word across fine-tuning generations 0 to 6. All three curves start near 3.2 and decline. The unfiltered and H_L curves drop fastest, to about 0.8 and 1.15 at generation 6. The green Ĥ_K curve stays clearly higher, ending near 1.4. Shaded bands and error bars show uncertainty. Panel (b) is a grouped bar chart of percent change versus the unfiltered baseline for Distinct-3, Vocabulary and Rep-4. The tall green bars carry '***' above them. The short blue bars are labeled 'ns', and the error bars on the blue bars cross zero. The eye goes first to the green curve and the tall green bars.
caption: Filtering on text-only entropy preserves diversity; logprob-based filtering does not. (a) Kontoyiannis entropy rate ˆHK across six fine-tuning generations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct under three training-data conditions: unfiltered (rapid collapse), HL-filtered (intermediate), and ˆHK-filtered (slowest decline). Shaded bands: ±1 SEM (n = 80 documents per generation). (b) Percentage change relative to the unfiltered baseline at generation 6 for three text-diversity metrics (Distinct-3, Vocabulary size, Rep-4). Error bars: bootstrap 95% CIs. ˆHK-based filtering yields highly significant improvements on all three metrics (∗∗∗p < 0.001), whereas HL-based filtering is non-significant on all three.
abstract: Iterative fine-tuning on synthetic data causes \emph{model collapse}: output diversity narrows as rare patterns are progressively lost, a signature most visible as phrase-level repetition. Existing mitigations either require model log-probabilities, an external oracle, or continued access to real human data. Here we develop a new approach grounded in mathematical information theory: the non-parametric Kontoyiannis entropy rate estimator $h_k$, computed entirely from raw text via match-length statistics, with no model of any kind. We show that this is in fact a \emph{superior} training-data filter on text-diversity metrics in a fully-synthetic, single-lineage fine-tuning setting. In a six-generation QLoRA collapse experiment on Llama-3.1-8B, logprob-based filtering (the most established model-access-requiring baseline) provides no significant text-diversity benefit on any metric ($p > 0.23$), whereas $h_k$-filtering yields $+42\%$ unique trigrams, $+30\%$ vocabulary, and $-19\%$ repetition (all $p < 0.001$). We validate $h_k$ as a cross-domain entropy proxy ($Î²= 0.924$, $R^2 = 0.746$) and collapse detector ($Ï= +0.454$, $p < 0.0001$) across 4~domains, 2~temperatures, 2~generator--scorer model pairs, and 1{,}520 generated documents. Our results demonstrate that information theoretic approaches to collapse mitigation are efficient, and suggest new approaches for maintaining multi-agent diversity.
